title: Venezuela Earthquake
change_caption: Red: brighter in the BEFORE image. Cyan: brighter in the AFTER image. Gray/white: little change. Black: no data. This compares image brightness, not measured ground motion.

radar_explainer.what_radar_sees: An earthquake can shift the ground, damage buildings and trigger landslides. Each of these changes how the radar signal bounces back, and comparing two dates can show where. Measuring centimeter-scale ground motion needs interferometry (InSAR), which this quicklook comparison does not show.
radar_explainer.polarization_note: The product contains HH and HV channels. The quicklook image does not tell us which channel it displays, so we make no polarization claim for this view.

This region lies on an active plate boundary, where the ground can suddenly slip and release energy.

story.summary: On June 24, 2026, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck Venezuela's northern coast, about 38 seconds after a magnitude 7.2 shock. The shaking was strongly felt in Caracas and caused significant damage across the Carabobo and Yaracuy regions.
story.nisar_insight: NISAR's L-band radar sees through clouds and works day and night, so it can image a disaster zone even when optical satellites cannot. Here, two images taken 12 days apart (17 and 29 June) bracket the earthquake, and the difference map shows where the radar signal changed.
story.looking_forward: NISAR revisits the same area roughly every 12 days. With processed data and interferometry, future studies could map ground deformation after earthquakes and help responders find the hardest-hit areas faster. Earthquakes themselves cannot be predicted.

decision.scenario: You're part of a disaster response team. Using the radar change map, you have limited resources to send rescue teams. Where do you send them first?

choices.text: The coastal area with the strongest signal change in the radar map
choices.feedback: A sensible start. Strong radar change can point to places where the ground or buildings were disturbed, so it helps decide where to look first. It is not a damage map though, so teams still need on-the-ground reports to confirm.

choices.text: The most densely populated city in the scene, even where the radar change is weaker
choices.feedback: Reasonable instinct. Population density matters because more people means more potential victims. The strongest approach combines radar change, population data and local reports.

choices.text: Wait for more satellite data before moving any teams
choices.feedback: Waiting has a cost, since every hour matters in rescue. NISAR revisits about every 12 days, so it supports planning and damage mapping, while the first response relies on field reports and faster sources.

caveat: Visual comparison of quicklook images, not a validated damage map. Scene covers the central-north coast; Caracas is outside the frame.
